titre: Lake Baikal, or the Ocean That Is Only Just Beginning
accroche: The deepest and oldest lake in the world is no ordinary hollow: it is a continental rift still in the process of opening.
contenu_vulgarise:
Standing on the ice of Lake Baikal in February, you are walking over 1,637 meters of water: enough to swallow four Eiffel Towers stacked beneath your feet. It is the greatest depth ever measured in a lake, and it owes nothing to a glacial accident.

## The Mechanism

Most large lakes sit in a hollow left behind by a glaciation or an ancient flood: a depression that is no longer growing. Baikal, in southern Siberia, is different: it occupies the Baikal Rift Zone, a fault where the continental crust is tearing apart. On one side, the Siberian craton, carried by the Eurasian plate; on the other, the Amur microplate. The two are moving apart by 3 to 4 millimeters a year, a seismological estimate. The lake floor is therefore not a hole waiting to be filled in: it is the floor of a rift that keeps sinking, faster than sediment can fill it.

This mechanism explains both Baikal's depth (1,637 meters, according to U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) measurements) and its age: the rift structures date back to the Oligocene and intensified from the Middle Pliocene onward, which makes it the oldest known freshwater lake. It also explains its volume: about 23,000 km³, roughly the equivalent of the five Great Lakes of North America combined, and about 20% of all the unfrozen surface fresh water on the planet held in a single basin.

## The Shift

A continental rift that opens is exactly the mechanism by which oceans are born: the Red Sea, which separates Africa from Arabia, was formed in the same way, only further along. The U.S. Geological Survey, for its part, sees it as a modern analog for the formation of ancient Atlantic-type continental margins: the first stage of a continental breakup that, elsewhere, ended up opening an ocean.

Nothing says the process will go all the way: the exact causes of the rifting are still debated, between a distant contribution from Pacific subduction and the effect of the collision between India and Eurasia. But the landmark changes the way you look at any deep lake: the question to ask is not only “how much water?” but “is the floor still moving?”

repere.texte: Baikal holds about 20% of the Earth's unfrozen surface fresh water (alone, more than the five Great Lakes of North America combined) in a basin that continues to widen by 3 to 4 mm every year.

carte.punch: The deepest of lakes is not a hole filled with water: it is an ocean that is only just beginning.
carte.idee: Baikal owes its depth of 1,637 meters and its millions of years of existence to an active continental rift: Eurasia and the Amur microplate are moving apart by 3 to 4 mm a year, carving out a basin faster than it fills in. The USGS sees it as a modern analog for the beginnings of an ocean.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Details the extension rates measured by seismology and by offsets in landforms, and the hypotheses about the origin of the rift.

quiz.question: Why is Lake Baikal both the deepest and the oldest freshwater lake in the world?
choix: Because a glacier carved an exceptionally deep trough during the last glaciation
Because it sits in an active continental rift, where the floor sinks faster than sediment fills it in
Because a meteorite impact formed a crater that erosion has never managed to fill
Because underwater hot springs keep sediment from settling on the bottom
quiz.explication: Baikal sits in the Baikal Rift Zone, where the Siberian craton and the Amur microplate have been moving apart by 3 to 4 mm a year since the Oligocene: the floor keeps sinking, which explains its record depth and exceptional age. A glacial lake or a meteorite crater, by contrast, fills in over time rather than deepening.

quiz_supplementaire.question: At what rate are the Siberian craton and the Amur microplate moving apart, and by what method was it established?
choix: 3 to 4 mm a year, by a seismological estimate
3 to 4 mm a year, by GPS measurements over several decades
10 cm a year, by recent satellite triangulation
1 mm a year, by a ground-based topographic survey
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The study by Radziminovich et al. 2013, cited by the entry, establishes this rate of 3 to 4 mm a year by seismology, not by GPS measurement.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What are the two hypotheses put forward to explain the cause of the Baikal rifting, which is still debated?
choix: An ancient meteorite and local volcanism that is now extinct
A distant contribution from Pacific subduction, and the collision between India and Eurasia
Recent global warming and the melting of nearby permafrost
A preexisting fault dating from the Precambrian, and nothing else
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that the exact causes of the rifting are still debated, between a distant contribution from Pacific subduction and the effect of the collision between India and Eurasia.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To what other geological phenomenon does the USGS compare the Baikal rift?
choix: A meteorite impact crater that has stayed active to this day
A subduction zone comparable to Japan's
The formation of ancient Atlantic-type continental margins, like the opening of the Red Sea
A shield volcano like those of Hawaii
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The USGS calls the Baikal rift a modern analog for the formation of ancient Atlantic continental margins, the same mechanism by which the Red Sea formed, only further along.
